title: Varicosities
path: Minor Disorders of Pregnancy and Management

headings.title: Understanding Varicosities During Pregnancy
headings.content: Varicosities are enlarged, twisted, and superficial veins that frequently develop or worsen during pregnancy. They most commonly appear in the lower extremities, though they can also affect the vulva and rectum. While often viewed primarily as a cosmetic nuisance, they represent a significant physical burden for pregnant women, causing aching pain, heaviness, and swelling that can disrupt daily activities and rest. Midwives in Nigerian clinical practice frequently encounter this complaint during routine antenatal visits, making it essential to differentiate normal physiological venous changes from pathological conditions like deep vein thrombosis.

headings.title: Why Pregnant Women Develop Varicose Veins: Anatomy and Physiology
headings.content:
The development of varicosities during gestation is driven by distinct anatomical and hormonal shifts. 

- **Progesterone elevation**: Hormones relax the smooth muscle walls of blood vessels, reducing venous tone.
- **Mechanical compression**: The growing gravid uterus places direct pressure on the inferior vena cava and pelvic veins, obstructing upward blood flow from the legs.
- **Increased blood volume**: Maternal plasma volume expands significantly to support the fetus, placing an extra load on the venous system.

Combined, these factors cause venous pressure to rise, stretching vein walls and forcing the delicate one-way valves to fail, leading to backward blood pooling.

headings.title: Common Sites Affected Beyond the Legs: Vulval and Hemorrhoidal Varicosities
headings.content: While lower limb veins bear the brunt of pregnancy-induced pressure, engorgement frequently occurs in other dependent areas. Vulval varicosities present as swollen, painful nodular densities on the labia majora or minora, often causing a heavy, dragging sensation in the perineum and discomfort during walking or intercourse. Hemorrhoids are varicose veins of the rectal and anal plexuses, heavily aggravated by both elevated venous pressure and the common pregnancy companion of constipation. Both sites usually resolve spontaneously postpartum, but require gentle local management to prevent acute distress.

headings.title: Clinical Presentation and Patient Complaints
headings.content: Pregnant women with varicose veins typically describe a dull, aching pain, a feeling of heavy or tired legs, and nocturnal muscle cramps in the calves. Symptoms usually worsen as the day progresses and after prolonged standing or sitting. Clinically, the affected veins appear bulging, dark purple or blue, and tortuous beneath the skin. Edema around the ankles often coexists. Patients may feel anxious about their appearance or discomfort, making empathetic clinical listening an important part of the assessment.

headings.title: Management of Varicose Veins in Pregnancy
headings.content: Conservative care is the cornerstone of managing varicose veins during pregnancy, as surgical interventions are generally deferred until after the puerperium unless severe complications arise. Midwives guide patients on non-invasive strategies aimed at improving venous return and reducing symptom severity. Compression therapy, postural adjustments, and gentle physical activity form the primary pillars of safe, effective antenatal care for this minor disorder.

headings.title: Counseling and Lifestyle Modifications for Midwives
headings.content:
Midwives play a vital teaching role by providing practical lifestyle advice during antenatal clinics. 

- **Avoid prolonged standing**: Encourage regular rest breaks with legs elevated.
- **Compression stockings**: Teach proper application of graduated support stockings before getting out of bed in the morning.
- **Positional habits**: Advise resting in the left lateral position to relieve inferior vena cava compression.
- **Exercise**: Recommend regular, gentle walking to activate the calf muscle pump.
- **Clothing choices**: Warn against wearing tight garters, knee-high socks with tight bands, or restrictive trousers that impede circulation.

headings.title: Potential Complications and When to Refer
headings.content: While most varicosities are benign, midwives must remain vigilant for rare but serious complications. Superficial thrombophlebitis—inflammation of a vein associated with a blood clot—causes localized pain, redness, and a hard, tender cord along the vein. Spontaneous rupture and severe hemorrhage from a vulval or leg varicosity is an emergency requiring immediate pressure and medical attention. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) must be suspected if unilateral leg swelling, marked pain, and warmth occur. Midwives must refer patients promptly to a medical officer or obstetrician when these red flags appear.
